newsitem.title: GERMANY: India's Chidambaram sees no inflation dangers.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram sees no inflation dangers.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said on Tuesday he did not see any current inflation dangers in the Indian economy and that he was not concerned by growing foreign reserves tied to the strengthening rupee.
Chidambaram, who said in mid-May he was against a stronger rupee because exporters would complain, on Tuesday told a news conference that liberalised trade policies must be implemented.
But he said the rupee would be defended from speculators.
"The reserve bank's policy is not to allow the rupee to be driven by speculators. Otherwise the value will be determined by the market," he said.
The rupee currently stands at about 36 to the dollar, and the central bank has had to intervene regularly to stop it appreciating due to growing pressure from investment inflows.
"We must liberalise trade. We must encourage more import of capitalised goods," Chidambaram said. "If industry picks up, then imports will pick up."
He said he was not concerned about growing foreign reserves in India, which now stand at about $24 billion.
"We must use these reserves creatively. We should not fall into a trap of reducing reserves. "We must use them to encourage trade and investment."

Chidambaram also said he was pleased that a committee appointed by the Indian central bank had voted in favour on Tuesday on his proposal to take steps needed to float the rupee as a fully convertible currency by the turn of the decade.
"You can be assured that I will allow for a wide discussion on the report and then make a decision as soon as possible," Chidambaram said of the report released on Tuesday in India.

Asked how he would implement the report's recommendations, which charts a path for the rupee to be convertible by 2000, he replied, "I am determined to overcome all obstacles in all fields. We are reformers."
Chidambaram said Indian inflation remained in single digits at about six percent and he saw no reason for concern even though the government is considering raising petroleum prices.
"We hope to keep inflation at that level," he said of the annual inflation rate of 6.3 percent seen so far in the 1997/98 financial year that began on April 1.
"It might rise if we correct petroleum prices but it should then standardise," he said. "We believe investor and business confidence has improved."
Chidambaram noted the government raised petroleum prices last July, which prompted inflation to rise. But he said it then tapered off to end the year at 7.3 percent.
"Even if inflation rises as a result of some price increases, good management of money means we can bring that under control," he said.

The decision-making steering committee of India's ruling United Front is scheduled to meet next week to reach consensus on increasing oil prices, which is required to repay money owed to oil companies for selling products well below global prices.

The outstanding amount, called the oil pool deficit, totalled 155 billion rupees ($4.33 billion) at the end of March and is expected to rise to 245 billion rupees by the end of next March, according to government figures.
